message.content:
Lions (Panthera leo) and zebras (Equus quagga) belong to two very different mammalian orders—Carnivora and Perissodactyla, respectively.  
Their most recent common ancestor is therefore the last common ancestor of the entire clade that contains both of those orders, i.e. the clade **Laurasiatheria**.

* **Laurasiatheria** is a major grouping of placental mammals that also includes Cetartiodactyla (whales, hippos, deer, pigs, etc.), Chiroptera (bats), and Eulipotyphla (hedgehogs, moles, shrews).  
* The last common ancestor of Laurasiatheria is estimated to have lived roughly **70–80 million years ago**, during the late Cretaceous period, after the breakup of the supercontinent Pangaea but before the full separation of Laurasia and Gondwana.

So, the common ancestor of a lion and a zebra is a mammal that lived about 70–80 million years ago and was the last common ancestor of the Laurasiatherian clade.
